Treat each user’s HR@10 as a paired binary outcome, retaining identical users and 99 fixed unique negatives across models. Recommended analysis: report per-category hit gains/losses and macro improvement Δ = ¼Σ(mean paired hit difference). Bootstrap paired users within each category for a 95% interval, preserving equal category weights; use exact McNemar tests for category comparisons or paired randomization for the macro statistic. One changed hit moves category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points. These intervals concern user sampling conditional on fitted models and candidate sets, excluding training-seed and negative-sampling uncertainty. [Dietterich](https://doi.org/10.1162/089976698300017197), [paired bootstrap](https://people.csail.mit.edu/people/koehn/publications/bootstrap2004.pdf).

For diagnostic comparisons, freeze candidate IDs, history truncation, masking and tie handling; inspect paired hit flips, positive ranks and score margins. Resampling negatives between checkpoints confounds model changes with candidate difficulty. Fixed negatives improve comparability but cannot establish full-catalog performance: sampled top-k metrics can reverse model order even in expectation. Full-catalog unseen-item recommendations for 20 training users therefore provide qualitative diagnostics, not an estimate of benchmark validation HR or population recommendation quality. [Krichene–Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/).

Repeated configuration and checkpoint selection creates winner’s optimism; an ordinary bootstrap interval around the selected winner does not correct it. Within the fixed GPU budget, predeclare evaluation cadence, maximum trials, stopping rules and a practical improvement threshold; log every validation look and compare candidates at matched compute. Bootstrap selection frequencies across logged candidates can describe winner instability, but remain exploratory after adaptive search. Preserve the untouched final evaluation for confirmation; never use test results for selection. [Cawley–Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html).
